SSE Renwables £80M upgrade of Lochay Hydro Power Station
As Principal Contractor for SSE Renewables at Lochay Hydro Power Station in Killin, Global Infrastructure is delivering the planning, coordination, and safe execution of works within a live hydroelectric generation environment. The project forms part of SSE Renewables' programme to repower the station with modern, more efficient turbine technology, extending its operational life by at least a further 40 years.
On site, Global Infrastructure has also been carrying out all civil works, incorporating old and new systems to ensure the asset is in its optimal position. There are three turbines within the power station, two major and one minor. Originally built around 1958, they have been in continuous operation and are now being upgraded to extend their lifespan. The disposal and dismantle phase has included the removal of existing turbines, generators, and ancillary components.
The main portion of the works has involved the partial removal of an existing concrete foundation and the construction of a new concrete plinth, including a 20T embedded plate for a new generator. This has required concrete cutting using wire ropes, intricate reinforcement, and Complex formwork Due to the nature of a water- driven turbine, achieving very fine tolerances is critical, as any deviation can lead to vibration issues.
The project was started in April 2025 with the immediate removal of one turbine, generator and associated equipment. Civils works to rebuild the foundation were completed in March 2026 and the full mechanical rebuild completed and No.1 Hydro Turbine returned to service. The second turbine will start being dismantled in April 2027.
Lochay Power Station will be commissioned with an unrated export conocity of 51MW (from 45MW) and will be be connected via a new substation. This substation forms part of a separate project currently being delivered for SSEN Transmission, which is progressing through construction.
SSE Renewables reached a major milestone in November 2026 by commissioning and returning the first of two new turbine generating units to commercial operation as part of an £80 million upgrade and repowering of the Lochay Hydro Power Station in Killin, Perthshire.
Project Overview
• Location: Killin, Perthshire, Scotland (part of the Breadalbane hydro scheme, originally commissioned in 1958).
• Investment: £80 million refurbishment.
• Lifespan Extension: Extends the station's operational life by 40+ years.
• Timeline: The full repowering project is scheduled for completion in 2028, coinciding with the facility's 70th anniversary.
Key Details & Scope
• Modernization: Replacing main generation components with modern, higher-efficiency turbine technology while retaining the historic 1950s civil infrastructure.
• Contractors: Voith Hydro (lead mechanical and electrical), Global Infrastructure (enabling works), AJT Engineering and Jack Tighe (penstock), Stantec (civil design), Konecranes Demag UK (crane), and McDonald Scaffolding.
• Economic Impact: Supports regional supply chains and local jobs (including peak construction jobs).— at Glen Lochay.

records.bodyText:
The Stronelairg Wind Farm is a major onshore renewable energy facility located in the Scottish Highlands.
Key Overview & Specifications
• Location: High up on a remote plateau in the Monadhliath Mountains near Fort Augustus, south-east of Loch Ness (Highland, Scotland), at an elevation of roughly 600 meters above sea level.
• Capacity & Turbines: Features 66 Vestas wind turbines with a total installed generating capacity of 228 MW (227.7 MW official rating).
• Commissioning: Fully operational since December 2018.
• Ownership: Developed and operated by SSE Renewables (50.1%) alongside co-owner Greencoat UK Wind Plc (49.9%).
• Integration: Co-located next to the existing Glendoe Hydroelectric Scheme, allowing both projects to share core electrical and access infrastructure.
The project faced a prolonged and contentious planning battle. Conservation groups—including the John Muir Trust and Mountaineering Scotland—launched legal challenges arguing that industrializing the high central plateau would damage the character of Scotland's designated wild land.
After initial court rulings went against the project, Scotland's Inner House of the Court of Session overturned the blocks in 2016, clearing the way for construction. Developers countered that the adjacent Glendoe hydro site already altered the immediate footprint, reducing its status as pristine wild land.
Through the Stronelairg Community Fund, roughly £569,250 is directed to local community and charitable initiatives each year, with an estimated £28 million projected over the lifespan of the project (2017–2042).
Additional funding feeds into a biennial Highland-wide Sustainable Development Fund.
Stronelairg sits at an elevation of around 600m above sea level in the Moadhliath Mountain range making it one of SSE windiest wind farms.
It sits within a natural bowl on a plateau, set well back from Loch Ness meaning that no turbines are visible from the main tourist routes in the area.  Stronelairg is also located adjacent to our 100MW Glendoe hydro scheme and so the construction teams were able to use the hydro infrastructure as do our operational teams now.
Construction began in late 2016 and the wind farm became operational in December 2018, six months ahead of schedule.
In February 2019, SSE agreed the sale of 49.9% of Stronelairg (and the Dunmaglass wind farm) to Greencoat UK Wind Plc
Global Infrastructure acted as Principle Contractor for SSE Renewables in 2024 on removing a steel arch culvert on the access road to Stronelairg Wind Farm.
The culvert was damaged during a flood event in June 2023, and replaced it with 12 no. box culvert sections with a headwall at either end.
The access road had a live HV and Fibre cable running adjacent to it in the verge. A temporary cable bridge was installed which supported these cables throughout the job. Contractors involved in the replacement culvert included:
• Civil and temporary works design was carried out by CS Eng (Group) Ltd www.csenggroup.co.uk.
• Contract lift was completed by @stoddartcranehire .
• Culverts supplied by FP McCann.— at Monadhliath Mountains.

Windy Standard III developed by Brockloch Rig III Ltd. received planning approval in March 2021 to construct and operate Windy Standard III. The 20-turbine project is an extension to Windy Standard I and Windy Standard. The project comprises the northern Meaul Hill Cluster with 12 x 177.5m turbines and the southern Waterhead Hill cluster with 8 x 125m turbines.
The wind farm extension is located in Carsphairn Forest, Dumfries and Galloway (Postcode DG7 3UP).
Situated north-east of Carsphairn and south of New Cumnock.(Coordinates: Latitude 55° 12' 42.1" N, Longitude -4° 15' 35.8" W (or approximately 55.106163, -4.1629523).
The project is now in construction and the team are working to discharge the associated planning conditions. To ensure that the site can be delivered efficiently and can achieve the greatest capacity, a later application was made to the Scottish Government to vary the consent - proposing to increase the tip height of the 12 turbines in the northern Meaul Hill Cluster to 180m to tip. This allows us to bring forward the site using readily available turbine technology.
It is envisaged that Windy Standard III will be commissioned in December 2026.
More information about the Windy Standard Wind Farm can be found at windystandardwindfarm.co.uk
Collett & Sons Ltd have successfully delivered 344 turbine components to Windy Standard III Wind Farm Extension in Dumfries and Galloway, supporting the construction of 20 ENERCON turbines.
Working from Glasgow and Ayr, the team completed the two-phase programme with loads including 68-metre blades and tower sections weighing up to 81 Tonnes. Theie Nooteboom Super Wing Carriers, tower clamp trailers and step- frame trailers were utlisised across the deliveries.
From vessel discharges to night-time deliveries, their skill and commitment helped overcome roadworks, tight junctions and access restrictions to get the components to site.
Windy Standard III onshore wind farm extension in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland, features 20 Enercon wind turbines totaling an 87.6 MW capacity:
The Wind Turbine Generators are:
12 x Enercon E-138 EP3 E3 turbines (Meaul Hill cluster), rated at 4.26 MW each and operating in a 4.5 MW Yield Optimised Mode on 111 m steel towers.
8 x Enercon E-115 EP3 turbines (Waterhead Hill cluster). 
The project is developed by Fred. Olsen Renewables, with component deliveries completed by Collett Transport in late 2026 ahead of its scheduled commissioning. Full specifications for the main turbine model can be reviewed on the Enercon E-138 EP3
Product Page.— in Carsphairn.

The UK government has signalled that future energy generation projects including Scotland's flagship ScotWind and floating offshore wind developments may not receive backing unless they can prove they deliver cheaper energy and have guaranteed grid connections
UK Energy and Treasury officials, including Chancellor John Healey and minister Dan Tomlinson, stated that future project approvals will depend on whether they bring cheaper energy and can reliably connect to the grid.
Around 60% of ScotWind proposals involve floating offshore wind, which faces severe hurdles and potential contract culls due to delayed transmission upgrades and high infrastructure costs.
Critics warn that the new framework could pivot support away from northern waters toward projects sitting closer to south-east England with more advanced or accessible grid infrastructure.
SNP energy ministers and industry leaders have accused Westminster of an "attack" on Scotland's renewables sector, warning that a lack of grid certainty risks stranding Scottish ports and losing billions in investment. https://www.scotsman.com/news/politics/scotland-north-sea-offshore-wind-scotwind-9350805

Scotsman letters
An interesting take on events from Joyce Mcmillan (“As climate change hits food security, parties backslide on net zero”, Perspective, 13 November), and as imaginative as usual.
She mentions how Kellogg’s announced that Rice Krispies “on this side of the Atlantic will no longer be made from whole rice grains” and cites the company claiming that “changing weather” in Europe is the cause. It would help if she had explained that the company who make Rice Krispies in Europe is a different company from the US Kellogg’s and that the US end continues to use rice! “Climate change” is the cause, she says.
Regarding the regular supplies to which consumers “have become accustomed over the last 80 years”, reports from earlier decades show the rice crop (amongst others) regularly suffered from what the Press & Journal in 1938 called the weather “playing pranks”, with wildly varying rainfall, droughts etc. It isn’t some recent development.
At least the latest COP she mentioned didn’t chop down virgin rainforest, or build motorways through it like last year’s. There will only be 92,000 delegates there, readers will be pleased to learn, but they will still have their big cars, their “aides” and their hotel aircon, you can bet. The only leader to attend is Andy Burnham, so little importance is attached to it by the people it’s supposed to make change their ways.
Andrew HN Gray Edinburgh

Orkney Link is a major 220 kV high-voltage alternating current (HVAC) transmission connection built by SSEN Transmission to connect the Orkney Islands to the national grid network for the first time.
Key Project Details
• Interconnector capacity up to 220 MW of renewable electricity transmission.
• Route connected a new substation at Finstown in Orkney to the Dounreay West Substation in Caithness, Scotland.
• Cable Scope: Approximately 69 km total length, including a 53 km subsea cable across the Pentland Firth, plus underground land cables in Orkney and Caithness. 
• Construction began in late 2024, subsea cable manufacturing and testing milestones were reached through 2025 and 2026, and full energization is targeted for 2028.
• Development unlocks the potential wind, tidal, and marine renewable energy from Orkney to help feed the UK's Net Zero targets.
You can track updates or view the interactive layout major milestone achieved for the Orkney Link project
Nexans has successfully completed the Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) of the 220 kV subsea cable for the Orkney Link project, marking a significant milestone in the delivery of this important electricity transmission infrastructure.
The successful completion of the FAT testing represents the culmination of more than a year of manufacturing activities at Nexans' facility in Halden, Norway.
Developed by SSEN Transmission, the Orkney Link is a 220 kV HVAC connection between Finstown in Orkney and Dounreay in Caithness, Scotland. Featuring approximately 53 km of subsea cable and a transmission capacity of up to 220 MW, the link will play a key role in unlocking Orkney's renewable energy potential and strengthening Scotland's electricity transmission network.
With this important manufacturing milestone achieved, project activities continue to progress on several fronts. Nexans' teams are currently advancing onshore cable installation and jointing works in Orkney, while preparations continue for the offshore installation campaign scheduled for 2027.— in Orkney Islands.
